officer.subject: £80m of your book at 1.5% out to 2070
officer.body:
Hi Sukvinder,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on your outturn report ahead of the Audit Committee sitting in September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. Your report is short and lays things out cleanly, including two indicators not met, which many reports would bury.

As a cross-check that our figures tie to yours before anything else: we hold 42 PWLB loans totalling £492.28m at a weighted 3.9177% for you at 31 March 2026. That is your paragraph 3 table less the £3.5m CMI, to the basis point.

What stands out in the shape of the book is the far end. Eighteen loans, £163m in aggregate, mature in 2050 or later at an average 2.93%. Four of those — £80m in principal, at 1.25% to 2.07%, all maturing March and April 2070 — are pandemic-era draws that today price around £52m below par on the DMO's premature repayment curve. Indicative only; the DMO's is the only binding quote and we model no MRP or accounting treatment. It is a striking low-cost tail in the book.

The other side is that the book grew £207.5m in one year. With that £163m of pre-2022 debt sitting at the back, the front of the book has come out shorter — 17% under 12 months against a 15% cap. The CFR came in £41m over the £856m limit as well. You've flagged both yourselves in the summary so we haven't gone looking for a hook there.

For a sense of where the curve has moved since your year-end: long end PWLB certainty rates are 0.11 to 0.19 higher today than at 31 March 2026; the one-year is 0.09 lower. All of your PWLB book is priced daily against the DMO's curve at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis, so the mark on those 2070 loans is a number you can look up on a Tuesday rather than commission. The monthly sector picture is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity: July was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers, average 5.02%.

On training, three look relevant to where H&F sits. Cost of carry and internal borrowing, for the £116.1m the HRA carries against a £559m CFR (paragraph 10). Debt rescheduling and premature repayment, given the shape of the tail. And our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. For members there's an Audit Committee Chair (Treasury) course, written for exactly the committee this report will next go to. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
